tool.name: Ruby on Rails
tool.tagline: Convention-over-configuration Ruby framework for full-stack web apps
tool.description: Ruby on Rails is a full-stack web framework built on the MVC pattern: Active Record for data, Action Controller and Action View for requests and HTML, Hotwire for interactive front ends, plus built-in jobs, mail, caching and WebSockets. Its conventions let small teams ship complete products quickly, and it runs companies like Shopify, GitHub and Basecamp. Rails 8 adds a built-in authentication generator, database-backed queues and caches, and Kamal deployments.

concepts.name: Creating an app and its conventions
concepts.summary: Generate a Rails 8 app, run it, and learn the directory layout and the conventions that make Rails work.
concepts.why: Rails' conventions are the framework: knowing them tells you where everything is and what you get for free.
concepts.body:
Install Rails with `gem install rails` and create an app with `rails new blog`. Rails 8 defaults are deliberately simple: SQLite in every environment, **Propshaft** for assets, **importmap** for JavaScript without a Node build step, **Hotwire** (Turbo and Stimulus), and the Solid trio (**Solid Queue**, **Solid Cache**, **Solid Cable**) backed by the database. It also generates a Dockerfile and **Kamal** config for deployment, plus RuboCop, Brakeman and a CI workflow.

Run `bin/dev` (or `bin/rails server`) and open `http://localhost:3000`.

The layout follows **MVC**:

- `app/models`, `app/controllers`, `app/views`: the three layers. Also `app/jobs`, `app/mailers`, `app/helpers` and `app/javascript`.
- `config/routes.rb` maps URLs; `config/database.yml` configures the database; `config/credentials.yml.enc` stores encrypted secrets.
- `db/migrate` and `db/schema.rb` hold the schema; `test/` holds tests; `bin/` holds binstubs like `bin/rails`.

**Convention over configuration** means names line up automatically: the `Article` model maps to the `articles` table, `ArticlesController` renders views from `app/views/articles/`, and `app/models/line_item.rb` defines `LineItem`. Follow the conventions and you write almost no glue code.

Generators create files that follow them: `bin/rails generate scaffold Article title:string body:text` produces a migration, model, controller, views, routes and tests. `bin/rails console` opens an IRB session with the app loaded.
concepts.code:
gem install rails
rails new blog            # SQLite, Hotwire, Propshaft, Solid Queue/Cache/Cable, Kamal
cd blog
bin/rails --version       # Rails 8.0.x

bin/rails generate scaffold Article title:string body:text published:boolean
bin/rails db:migrate
bin/dev                   # http://localhost:3000/articles

bin/rails console         # IRB with the app loaded
# >> Article.create!(title: "Hello", body: "First post")
# >> Article.count  # => 1

bin/rails routes -g article   # routes matching "article"
bin/rails test                # run the test suite
takeaways: rails new gives a complete, production-ready stack with database-backed defaults
Names connect layers: Article -> articles table -> ArticlesController -> views/articles
Generators and bin/rails console speed up everyday work
pitfalls: Fighting conventions (custom table names, odd file names) and then writing glue code Rails would have made unnecessary.

quiz.q: Following Rails conventions, which table does the model LineItem use?
quiz.explain: Model names are singular CamelCase; tables are plural snake_case.

concepts.name: Routing
concepts.summary: Map URLs to controller actions in config/routes.rb with resources, nested routes, root and named route helpers.
concepts.why: Routes define your app's URL design and generate the path helpers used throughout views and controllers.
concepts.body:
`config/routes.rb` maps HTTP verbs and paths to `controller#action`:

```ruby
Rails.application.routes.draw do
  root "articles#index"
  get "/about", to: "pages#about", as: :about
  resources :articles
end
```

`resources :articles` creates the seven RESTful routes: `index` (GET /articles), `new`, `create` (POST /articles), `show` (GET /articles/:id), `edit`, `update` (PATCH/PUT /articles/:id) and `destroy` (DELETE). Limit them with `only: [:index, :show]` or `except:`. Use `resource :profile` (singular) for things a user has only one of.

Every named route generates **path and URL helpers**: `articles_path` gives `/articles`, `article_path(@article)` gives `/articles/42`, `edit_article_path(@article)`, `new_article_path`, and `_url` versions with the host. Use them everywhere instead of literal strings.

Organising routes:

- **Nested** resources express ownership: `resources :articles do resources :comments, only: [:create, :destroy] end` gives `/articles/:article_id/comments`. Keep nesting one level deep (use `shallow: true` for deeper hierarchies).
- `member { post :publish }` adds `/articles/:id/publish`; `collection { get :search }` adds `/articles/search`.
- `namespace :admin do ... end` prefixes paths, helpers and controllers (`Admin::UsersController`).
- Dynamic segments and constraints: `get "/u/:username", to: "users#show", constraints: { username: /[a-z0-9_]+/ }`.

`bin/rails routes` lists everything, with `-g` to filter. Routes match top to bottom; the first match wins.
concepts.code:
# config/routes.rb
Rails.application.routes.draw do
  root "articles#index"

  resources :articles do
    member { post :publish }               # POST /articles/:id/publish
    collection { get :search }             # GET  /articles/search
    resources :comments, only: %i[create destroy]
  end

  resource :session                        # singular: /session
  get "/@:username", to: "profiles#show", as: :profile,
      constraints: { username: /[a-z0-9_]+/ }

  namespace :admin do
    resources :users, only: %i[index update]   # Admin::UsersController
  end

  get "up" => "rails/health#show", as: :rails_health_check
end

# Helpers: article_path(@article)              => "/articles/42"
#          article_comments_path(@article)      => "/articles/42/comments"
#          publish_article_path(@article)       => "/articles/42/publish"
#          profile_path(username: "ada")        => "/@ada"
takeaways: resources :things generates the seven RESTful routes and helpers
Use path helpers like article_path(@article) instead of literal URLs
Nest one level for ownership; use member, collection and namespace to organise
pitfalls: Deeply nesting resources, producing unwieldy URLs and helpers; prefer shallow nesting.

quiz.q: Which request does resources :articles map to ArticlesController#update?
quiz.explain: update is reached with PATCH (or PUT) on the member URL /articles/:id.

concepts.name: Controllers and actions
concepts.summary: Write controller actions that read params, load models, and render, redirect or respond with the right status.
concepts.why: Controllers coordinate every request, and knowing render versus redirect and callbacks avoids many beginner bugs.
concepts.body:
A controller is a class inheriting from `ApplicationController`; each public method is an **action**. After an action runs, Rails renders the template with the same name (`articles/show.html.erb` for `show`) unless you call `render` or `redirect_to` yourself. Instance variables set in the action (`@article`) are visible in the view.

`params` holds route segments, query-string values and form data in one hash-like object with indifferent access: `params[:id]` and `params["id"]` both work. Values are strings.

Responding:

- `render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity` renders another template in the same request (used to redisplay a form with errors). Turbo expects a 4xx status for failed form submissions.
- `redirect_to @article, notice: "Saved"` sends a 302 to a new URL; the notice is stored in the **flash** for the next request. Use `status: :see_other` (303) after a DELETE.
- `render json: @article`, `head :no_content`, `render plain: "ok"`.

A common bug is calling `render` or `redirect_to` twice in one action, which raises `DoubleRenderError`; add `return` after an early redirect.

**Callbacks** run around actions: `before_action :set_article, only: %i[show edit update destroy]` loads the record once for several actions. `rescue_from` handles exceptions per controller.

`Model.find(params[:id])` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` when missing, which Rails turns into a 404 in production. `session[:key]` and `cookies` persist data across requests.
concepts.code:
class ArticlesController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_article, only: %i[show edit update destroy]

  def index
    @articles = Article.order(created_at: :desc).limit(20)
  end

  def show; end   # renders app/views/articles/show.html.erb

  def update
    if @article.update(article_params)
      redirect_to @article, notice: "Article updated"
    else
      render :edit, status: :unprocessable_entity
    end
  end

  def destroy
    @article.destroy!
    redirect_to articles_path, notice: "Deleted", status: :see_other
  end
  private
  def set_article = @article = Article.find(params[:id])   # 404 if missing
  def article_params = params.expect(article: %i[title body])
end
takeaways: Actions render the template of the same name unless you render or redirect
render redisplays in the same request; redirect_to starts a new one
before_action shares setup like loading the record
pitfalls: Calling redirect_to and then continuing to code that renders, causing DoubleRenderError; return after redirecting.

quiz.q: A form submission fails validation. What is the conventional response?
quiz.explain: Rendering keeps the invalid object and its errors; the 422 status tells Turbo to display the response.

concepts.name: Views, layouts and partials
concepts.summary: Render HTML with ERB templates, layouts and partials, and use helpers like link_to and the flash.
concepts.why: Views are what users see, and partials and helpers keep them consistent and DRY.
concepts.body:
Views are **ERB** templates in `app/views/<controller>/<action>.html.erb`. `<%= expr %>` outputs the result, **HTML-escaped** by default, which protects against XSS. `<% code %>` runs Ruby without output, for loops and conditionals. Avoid `raw` and `html_safe` on user input.

The **layout** `app/views/layouts/application.html.erb` wraps every page; `<%= yield %>` marks where the action's template goes. Templates can fill named regions with `content_for :title` and the layout reads them with `yield :title`.

**Partials** are reusable fragments whose file names start with an underscore: `_article.html.erb`. Render one with `<%= render "form", article: @article %>` or, for a collection, `<%= render @articles %>`, which renders `articles/_article` once per record with a local `article`. Collection rendering is faster than looping and calling `render` yourself.

**Helpers** are Ruby methods available in views:

- `link_to "Edit", edit_article_path(@article)` and `button_to "Delete", @article, method: :delete`.
- `image_tag`, `time_ago_in_words`, `pluralize(3, "comment")`, `number_to_currency`, `truncate`, `simple_format`.
- Your own in `app/helpers`.

Show flash messages in the layout with `notice` and `alert`. Use `dom_id(@article)` for consistent element ids, which Turbo uses as well. Keep logic out of views: compute data in the controller or a model method and give the view simple values.
concepts.code:
<%# app/views/layouts/application.html.erb %> <%= content_for(:title) || "Blog" %> <% if notice %>

<%= notice %>

<% end %> <%= yield %> <%# app/views/articles/index.html.erb %> <% content_for :title, "All articles" %>

Articles (<%= pluralize(@articles.size, "article") %>)

<%= render @articles %> <%# renders _article.html.erb for each %> <%= link_to "New article", new_article_path %> <%# app/views/articles/_article.html.erb %>

<%= link_to article.title, article %>

<%= truncate(article.body, length: 120) %>

<%= time_ago_in_words(article.created_at) %> ago
takeaways: <%= %> outputs escaped HTML; <% %> runs code
Layouts wrap pages via yield; partials (_name) are reusable fragments
render @collection renders a partial per record efficiently
pitfalls: Calling html_safe or raw on user-supplied content, which disables escaping and allows XSS.

quiz.q: What does <%= render @articles %> do?
quiz.explain: Rendering a collection uses the model's partial path, articles/_article, for each element.

concepts.name: Migrations and the schema
concepts.summary: Evolve the database with migrations, references and indexes, and understand schema.rb.
concepts.why: Migrations keep every environment's database in sync and are part of every Rails feature you build.
concepts.body:
A **migration** is a Ruby class in `db/migrate` that changes the schema. Generate one with a descriptive name and Rails pre-fills it:

```bash
bin/rails generate migration AddPublishedAtToArticles published_at:datetime:index
bin/rails generate model Comment article:references body:text
```

The `change` method describes the change, and Rails knows how to reverse most operations automatically:

- `create_table :comments do |t| ... t.timestamps end`. Tables get an `id` primary key by default.
- `t.references :article, null: false, foreign_key: true` adds `article_id`, an index and a foreign key constraint.
- `add_column`, `remove_column` (give the type so it stays reversible), `rename_column`, `add_index :users, :email, unique: true`, `change_column_null`, `change_column_default`.
- For irreversible changes, write `up` and `down`, or use `reversible do |dir| ... end`.

Run `bin/rails db:migrate`; `db:rollback` undoes the last one; `db:migrate:status` shows state. `db:prepare` creates and migrates as needed, which is useful in deploy scripts.

After migrating, Rails dumps the full current schema to `db/schema.rb`. Commit it: it is the authoritative description of the database, and `db:schema:load` builds a fresh database from it far faster than replaying every migration.

Enforce integrity in the database too: `null: false`, unique indexes and foreign keys catch bugs that model validations miss, such as race conditions.
concepts.code:
# db/migrate/20250601120000_create_comments.rb
class CreateComments < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.0]
  def change
    create_table :comments do |t|
      t.references :article, null: false, foreign_key: true
      t.references :user, null: false, foreign_key: true
      t.text :body, null: false
      t.timestamps
    end
    add_index :comments, [:article_id, :created_at]
  end
end

# db/migrate/20250602090000_add_slug_to_articles.rb
class AddSlugToArticles < ActiveRecord::Migration[8.0]
  def change
    add_column :articles, :slug, :string
    add_index :articles, :slug, unique: true
  end
end

# $ bin/rails db:migrate      -> updates db/schema.rb
# $ bin/rails db:rollback     -> reverses AddSlugToArticles automatically
takeaways: Write changes in change; Rails reverses most of them automatically
t.references with foreign_key: true adds the column, index and constraint
Commit db/schema.rb; it is the authoritative schema
pitfalls: Editing a migration that already ran on other machines instead of adding a new one.

quiz.q: What does t.references :article, foreign_key: true create?
options: An article_id column, an index on it and a foreign key to articles
quiz.explain: references adds article_id with an index by default, and foreign_key: true adds the constraint.

concepts.name: Active Record basics
concepts.summary: Create, read, update and delete records with Active Record, and build lazy, chainable queries.
concepts.why: Active Record is how Rails apps talk to the database, and its query interface is used in nearly every file.
concepts.body:
A model is a class inheriting from `ApplicationRecord`. Active Record reads the table's columns and creates attribute methods automatically, so `class Article < ApplicationRecord; end` is a complete model.

**Create**: `Article.new(title: "Hi")` then `save`, or `Article.create(...)`. **Read**: `find(id)` (raises `RecordNotFound`), `find_by(slug: "hi")` (returns nil), `first`, `last`, `all`. **Update**: `article.update(title: "New")`. **Delete**: `article.destroy` (runs callbacks) or `delete_all`/`destroy_all` on a relation.

Bang methods (`save!`, `create!`, `update!`) raise on validation failure; the plain versions return false. Use bang versions where failure would be a bug, such as in scripts and jobs.

Queries chain into a **relation**, which is lazy: no SQL runs until you iterate, call `to_a`, `first`, `count` or similar.

```ruby
Article.where(published: true).where("created_at > ?", 1.week.ago).order(created_at: :desc).limit(10)
```

- Hash conditions (`where(status: "draft")`, `where(id: [1, 2])`, `where(created_at: 1.day.ago..)`) and `?` placeholders are safe. Never interpolate input into SQL strings.
- `where.not(...)`, `or(...)`, `select`, `distinct`, `group`, `having`.
- `pluck(:title)` returns plain values without building model objects; `exists?` and `count` run cheap queries.
- `find_each` iterates in batches of 1000 for big tables.

`.to_sql` shows the SQL a relation will run, and the console logs every query.
concepts.code:
article = Article.create!(title: "Hello Rails", body: "First", published: true)
article.update!(title: "Hello again")
p article.persisted?                     # true

recent = Article.where(published: true)
                .where(created_at: 1.week.ago..)
                .order(created_at: :desc)
                .limit(5)                # nothing queried yet
puts recent.to_sql
# SELECT "articles".* FROM "articles" WHERE "articles"."published" = 1
#   AND "articles"."created_at" >= '...' ORDER BY ... LIMIT 5
p recent.map(&:title)                    # query runs here

p Article.find_by(title: "nope")         # nil
p Article.where(published: false).count  # SELECT COUNT(*) ...
p Article.pluck(:id, :title).first       # [1, "Hello again"]

term = "Rails"
Article.where("title LIKE ?", "%#{term}%")   # safe: bound parameter
Article.find_each(batch_size: 500) { |a| a.touch }
takeaways: Models map to tables; attributes come from columns automatically
Relations are lazy and chainable; SQL runs when results are needed
Use hash conditions or ? placeholders, never string interpolation
pitfalls: Writing where("title = '#{params[:q]}'"), which is a SQL injection vulnerability.

quiz.q: When does Article.where(published: true).order(:title) hit the database?
options: When the results are needed, e.g. each, to_a or first
quiz.explain: Relations are lazy; enumerating or loading them triggers the query.

concepts.name: Forms and strong parameters
concepts.summary: Build forms with form_with, show validation errors, and whitelist input with params.expect.
concepts.why: Forms are how users change data, and strong parameters are Rails' guard against mass-assignment attacks.
concepts.body:
`form_with(model: @article)` builds a form bound to a model. Rails picks the URL and method by convention: POST to `/articles` for a new record, PATCH to `/articles/:id` for an existing one. Inside the block, field helpers name inputs `article[title]` and pre-fill current values:

```erb
<%= form_with model: @article do |f| %>
  <%= f.label :title %>
  <%= f.text_field :title %>
  <%= f.text_area :body %>
  <%= f.submit %>
<% end %>
```

Other helpers: `f.select`, `f.check_box`, `f.date_field`, `f.email_field`, `f.file_field`, `f.collection_select`. The form includes a hidden **CSRF token**, which Rails verifies on every non-GET request.

Display validation errors with `@article.errors.full_messages`, or per field with `@article.errors[:title]`. Invalid fields are wrapped in a `field_with_errors` div for styling.

The submitted data arrives nested: `params[:article][:title]`. Passing raw params to `create` or `update` would let an attacker set any attribute, such as `admin: true`, so Rails refuses unpermitted params. **Strong parameters** whitelist what's allowed. Rails 8 adds `params.expect`, which also checks the shape and returns a 400 for malformed input:

```ruby
params.expect(article: [:title, :body, tag_ids: []])
```

The older equivalent is `params.require(:article).permit(:title, :body, tag_ids: [])`. Arrays and nested hashes must be declared explicitly.
concepts.code:
# app/controllers/articles_controller.rb def new @article = Article.new end def create @article = Current.user.articles.new(article_params) if @article.save redirect_to @article, notice: "Published!" else render :new, status: :unprocessable_entity end end private def article_params # Rails 8: whitelist and check the shape in one call params.expect(article: [:title, :body, :category_id, tag_ids: []]) end # Submitted: { article: { title: "Hi", body: "...", admin: "1" } } # -> admin is filtered out; a non-hash article param -> 400 Bad Request # app/views/articles/_form.html.erb (excerpt) # <% if article.errors.any? %> #
    <% article.errors.full_messages.each do |m| %>
  • <%= m %>
    • <% end %>
# <% end %>
takeaways: form_with(model:) picks the URL, method and field values by convention
Strong parameters whitelist attributes before mass assignment
params.expect (Rails 8) checks shape too and returns 400 for bad input
pitfalls: Forgetting to permit array params like tag_ids: [], so they are silently dropped.

quiz.q: Why does Article.create(params[:article]) raise ForbiddenAttributesError?
options: Unfiltered params can't be mass-assigned; you must permit attributes first
quiz.explain: Rails blocks mass assignment of unpermitted parameters to prevent attackers setting arbitrary columns.

concepts.name: Validations and callbacks
concepts.summary: Validate models before saving, read errors, and use lifecycle callbacks carefully.
concepts.why: Validations keep bad data out, and misused callbacks are one of the most common sources of Rails bugs.
concepts.body:
**Validations** run when you call `save`, `create`, `update` or `valid?`. If any fails, nothing is written and `errors` is populated:

```ruby
validates :title, presence: true, length: { maximum: 120 }
validates :slug, uniqueness: { case_sensitive: false }, format: { with: /\A[a-z0-9-]+\z/ }
validates :price, numericality: { greater_than_or_equal_to: 0 }
```

Other built-ins: `inclusion: { in: %w[draft published] }`, `comparison`, `acceptance`, `confirmation`. Add `allow_nil: true`, `if:`/`unless:` and `on: :create` to scope them. For custom logic, write `validate :method_name` and call `errors.add(:field, "message")`.

`uniqueness` checks with a SELECT before inserting, so two concurrent requests can both pass. Always back it with a **unique index** in the database.

**Callbacks** hook into the lifecycle: `before_validation`, `before_save`, `after_create`, `before_destroy`, and the transaction-aware `after_commit` (with shortcuts `after_create_commit` and `after_update_commit`). Good uses are small, model-local concerns: normalising data before validation (Rails 7.1+ also has `normalizes :email, with: -> { it.strip.downcase }`) or setting derived fields.

Rules for callbacks:

- Use `after_commit` (not `after_save`) for side effects like enqueueing jobs or sending email, so they don't fire for rolled-back transactions.
- Don't put cross-model workflows in callbacks; an explicit method or service object is easier to follow and test.
- Methods like `update_column`, `update_all` and `insert_all` skip validations and callbacks.
concepts.code:
class Article < ApplicationRecord
  normalizes :slug, with: -> { it.strip.downcase }

  validates :title, presence: true, length: { maximum: 120 }
  validates :slug, presence: true, uniqueness: true,
                   format: { with: /\A[a-z0-9-]+\z/, message: "only a-z, 0-9 and -" }
  validate :publish_date_not_in_past, if: :published?

  before_validation :generate_slug, on: :create
  after_create_commit -> { NotifyFollowersJob.perform_later(self) }

  private

  def generate_slug = self.slug ||= title.to_s.parameterize
  def publish_date_not_in_past
    errors.add(:published_at, "can't be in the past") if published_at&.past?
  end
end

a = Article.new(title: "", slug: "Bad Slug!")
a.valid?                       # => false
a.errors.full_messages
# => ["Title can't be blank", "Slug only a-z, 0-9 and -"]
Article.create!(title: "Hello World")   # slug "hello-world"; job enqueued after commit
takeaways: save and valid? run validations; errors explains failures
Back uniqueness validations with a unique database index
Use after_commit for side effects; keep callbacks small and local
pitfalls: Sending emails or enqueueing jobs in after_save, which fires even if the transaction later rolls back.

quiz.q: Why can validates :email, uniqueness: true still allow duplicates?
options: Two concurrent requests can both check before either inserts
quiz.explain: The check is a separate SELECT; only a unique index makes the database reject the race.

concepts.name: Associations and eager loading
concepts.summary: Connect models with belongs_to, has_many and has_many :through, and prevent N+1 queries with includes.
concepts.why: Real domains are relational, and N+1 queries are the most common Rails performance problem.
concepts.body:
**Associations** declare relationships and generate methods:

- `belongs_to :author, class_name: "User"` on the model holding the foreign key (`author_id`). Since Rails 5 it is **required** by default; use `optional: true` otherwise.
- `has_many :comments, dependent: :destroy` on the other side. `dependent:` decides what happens to children when the parent is destroyed.
- `has_one :profile`.
- `has_many :tags, through: :taggings` for many-to-many via a join model, which can carry its own columns. `has_and_belongs_to_many` exists but a join model is more flexible.
- Polymorphic: `belongs_to :commentable, polymorphic: true`.

Generated methods include `article.comments` (a relation you can chain: `article.comments.where(approved: true)`), `article.comments.create!(...)` (sets the foreign key), `comment.article`, `article.tag_ids = [1, 2]`. `counter_cache: true` on `belongs_to` keeps a `comments_count` column up to date.

The **N+1 problem**: listing 50 articles and calling `article.author.name` in the view runs 51 queries. Fix it by eager loading:

- `includes(:author, comments: :user)` lets Rails choose between separate queries and a JOIN.
- `preload` always uses separate queries; `eager_load` always uses a LEFT OUTER JOIN (needed when you filter on the association).
- `joins(:comments)` is for filtering only and doesn't load the association.

Turn on `strict_loading` (per model, per query or app-wide) to raise on lazy loads during development.
concepts.code:
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :articles, foreign_key: :author_id, inverse_of: :author
end

class Article < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :author, class_name: "User"
  has_many :comments, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :taggings, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :tags, through: :taggings
end

class Comment < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :article, counter_cache: true   # needs articles.comments_count
  belongs_to :user
end

# N+1: 1 query for articles + 1 per article for its author
Article.limit(50).each { |a| puts a.author.name }

# Eager loaded: 3 queries total
Article.includes(:author, :tags).limit(50).each do |a|
  puts "#{a.title} by #{a.author.name} [#{a.tags.map(&:name).join(', ')}] #{a.comments_count}"
end
Article.joins(:tags).where(tags: { name: "rails" }).distinct   # filter only
Article.strict_loading.first.author   # raises ActiveRecord::StrictLoadingViolationError
takeaways: belongs_to holds the foreign key and is required by default
has_many :through models many-to-many with a real join model
includes/preload/eager_load fix N+1; joins only filters
pitfalls: Calling association methods inside a loop over records loaded without includes.

quiz.q: You need articles WHERE tags.name = 'rails', and you also display each article's tags. Which is right?
quiz.explain: Filtering on the association needs it in the JOIN, and eager_load both joins and loads it.

quiz.q: What does belongs_to :author do if author_id is nil when saving (Rails 5+)?
options: Adds a validation error: Author must exist
quiz.explain: belongs_to is required by default unless you pass optional: true.

concepts.name: Scopes and advanced queries
concepts.summary: Name reusable queries with scopes and class methods, and use joins, grouping, merges and batching.
concepts.why: Named scopes turn scattered query fragments into a readable, composable vocabulary for your domain.
concepts.body:
A **scope** names a query fragment on the model:

```ruby
scope :published, -> { where(published: true) }
scope :recent, ->(days = 7) { where(created_at: days.days.ago..) }
```

Scopes always return a relation, so they chain: `Article.published.recent(30).order(:title)`. They also work through associations: `user.articles.published`. A class method that returns a relation works the same way; scopes are just shorter, and a scope whose body returns nil returns `all` instead, keeping chains safe.

Avoid `default_scope`: it silently applies everywhere, including to associations and new records, and is hard to escape.

More query tools:

- `merge(OtherModel.scope)` reuses another model's scope inside a join: `Article.joins(:author).merge(User.active)`.
- `group(:category_id).count` returns a hash like `{1 => 12, 2 => 5}`; `sum`, `average`, `maximum` work the same way.
- `left_joins(:comments).where(comments: { id: nil })` finds records without children; `where.missing(:comments)` is shorthand.
- `or`, `not`, `rewhere`, `unscope`, `extending`.
- `in_batches(of: 1000).update_all(...)` changes large sets in chunks; `insert_all` and `upsert_all` write many rows in one statement (skipping validations and callbacks).
- `Article.where(...).explain` shows the database's query plan.

For SQL that is easier written raw, `find_by_sql` and `select("...")` remain available, still with bound parameters.
concepts.code:
class Article < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :author, class_name: "User"
  has_many :comments

  scope :published, -> { where(published: true) }
  scope :recent, ->(days = 7) { where(created_at: days.days.ago..) }
  scope :by, ->(user) { where(author: user) if user }   # nil -> all
  scope :popular, -> { joins(:comments).group(:id).having("COUNT(comments.id) >= ?", 10) }
end

class User < ApplicationRecord
  scope :active, -> { where(active: true) }
end

Article.published.recent(30).by(nil).order(:title)   # by(nil) keeps the chain
Article.joins(:author).merge(User.active)             # reuse User's scope
Article.published.group(:category_id).count           # {1 => 12, 2 => 5}
Article.where.missing(:comments)                      # articles with no comments
Article.where(published: false).in_batches(of: 1000)
       .update_all(archived: true)                    # chunked set-based update
Article.upsert_all([{ slug: "a", title: "A" }], unique_by: :slug)
puts Article.published.recent.explain
takeaways: Scopes name reusable query fragments and always return relations
merge reuses another model's scopes across joins
group/count, where.missing, in_batches and upsert_all cover common bulk needs
pitfalls: Using default_scope, which leaks into every query and association.

quiz.q: What does a scope return if its lambda body evaluates to nil?
options: The model's all relation, so chaining still works
quiz.explain: Scopes guarantee a relation; a nil body is replaced with all.

concepts.name: Hotwire: Turbo and Stimulus
concepts.summary: Make server-rendered pages feel like an SPA with Turbo Drive, Frames and Streams, and sprinkle behaviour with Stimulus.
concepts.why: Hotwire is Rails' default front end: rich interactivity without writing or maintaining a JavaScript SPA.
concepts.body:
**Hotwire** sends HTML, not JSON, over the wire. It has two parts installed by default.

**Turbo** handles navigation and updates:

- **Turbo Drive** intercepts link clicks and form submissions, fetches the next page and swaps the body without a full reload. Failed form submissions must return a 4xx status (422) so Turbo renders the response. Turbo 8 can **morph** pages on refresh (`turbo_refreshes_with method: :morph`), keeping scroll and focus.
- **Turbo Frames** (`<%= turbo_frame_tag dom_id(article) do %>`) make a region update independently: links and forms inside a frame replace only that frame with the matching frame from the response. Lazy-load a frame with `src:` and `loading: :lazy`.
- **Turbo Streams** apply targeted changes: `append`, `prepend`, `replace`, `update`, `remove`, `before`, `after`, `refresh`. Respond with them from a controller (`format.turbo_stream`) or broadcast them to every subscriber over WebSockets from a model with `broadcasts_to` or `broadcast_append_to`, which uses Action Cable (Solid Cable by default).

**Stimulus** adds small bits of JavaScript behaviour to server-rendered HTML. A controller is a JS class connected through data attributes: `data-controller="clipboard"`, `data-action="click->clipboard#copy"` and `data-clipboard-target="source"`. State lives in the DOM, so controllers keep working after Turbo replaces content.

The workflow: start with plain server-rendered pages, add Frames for in-place editing, Streams for live updates, and Stimulus only for what HTML can't do.
concepts.code:
<%# app/views/comments/_comment.html.erb %> <%= turbo_frame_tag dom_id(comment) do %>

<%= comment.body %> <%= link_to "Edit", edit_comment_path(comment) %>

<% end %> <%# Edit renders a form inside the same frame id: only this comment is replaced %> <%# app/views/articles/show.html.erb %> <%= turbo_stream_from @article %> <%# subscribe to live updates %>
<%= render @article.comments %>
<%# app/models/comment.rb: after_create_commit -> { broadcast_append_to article, target: "comments" } %> <%# app/views/comments/create.turbo_stream.erb %> <%= turbo_stream.append "comments", @comment %> <%= turbo_stream.update "comment_form", partial: "comments/form" %> <%# Stimulus: app/javascript/controllers/clipboard_controller.js export default class extends Controller { static targets = ["source"] copy() { navigator.clipboard.writeText(this.sourceTarget.value) } } %>
takeaways: Turbo Drive makes navigation fast; failed forms must return 422
Frames update one region; Streams append, replace or remove elements, even live via broadcasts
Stimulus connects small JS controllers to HTML with data attributes
pitfalls: Returning 200 for a failed form submission, so Turbo ignores the re-rendered form with errors.

quiz.q: A link inside turbo_frame_tag "comment_5" is clicked. What does Turbo do with the response?
options: Extracts the frame with id comment_5 and replaces only that frame
Appends the response to the frame
Opens it in a new tab
quiz.explain: Navigation inside a frame is scoped: Turbo swaps in the matching frame from the response.

concepts.name: Authentication with the Rails 8 generator
concepts.summary: Add sign-in with bin/rails generate authentication, has_secure_password, sessions and rate limiting.
concepts.why: Rails 8 ships its own authentication, so you can understand and own every line instead of relying on a large gem.
concepts.body:
Rails 8 includes an **authentication generator**: `bin/rails generate authentication`. It creates:

- A `User` model with `has_secure_password` and an `email_address` column, plus a `Session` model that stores each login (with IP and user agent) in the database.
- An `Authentication` concern included in `ApplicationController`, which requires login for every action by default. Opt out per controller with `allow_unauthenticated_access only: %i[index show]`.
- `SessionsController` for sign-in and sign-out, rate-limited with `rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create`, and `PasswordsController` with a mailer for password resets.
- `Current.user` and `Current.session`, available anywhere during a request through `Current` (an `ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes` class).

There is deliberately no sign-up flow; you add a registration controller that fits your app.

`has_secure_password` (needs the bcrypt gem) adds `password` and `password_confirmation` virtual attributes, stores a bcrypt `password_digest`, and provides `authenticate`. The generator uses `User.authenticate_by(email_address:, password:)`, which takes constant time whether or not the user exists, so attackers can't detect valid emails by timing.

The session id lives in a signed, `httponly` permanent cookie. Signing out destroys the `Session` row, which makes revoking all of a user's sessions easy.

For OAuth, add OmniAuth; Devise remains an option for apps that need many features out of the box. Authorization (who may do what) is separate: check ownership in controllers, e.g. `Current.user.articles.find(params[:id])`, or use a gem like Pundit.
concepts.code:
# $ bin/rails generate authentication && bin/rails db:migrate
# app/models/user.rb (generated)
class User < ApplicationRecord
  has_secure_password
  has_many :sessions, dependent: :destroy
  normalizes :email_address, with: ->(e) { e.strip.downcase }
end
# app/controllers/sessions_controller.rb (generated, abridged)
class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access only: %i[new create]
  rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create,
             with: -> { redirect_to new_session_url, alert: "Try again later." }
  def create
    if user = User.authenticate_by(params.permit(:email_address, :password))
      start_new_session_for user
      redirect_to after_authentication_url
    else
      redirect_to new_session_path, alert: "Try another email address or password."
    end
  end
end
# Your controllers: scope records to the signed-in user (authorization)
class ArticlesController < ApplicationController
  def edit = @article = Current.user.articles.find(params[:id])   # 404 for others' articles
end
takeaways: bin/rails generate authentication creates User, Session, controllers and the Authentication concern
Every action requires login unless allow_unauthenticated_access is used
authenticate_by and rate_limit defend against timing and brute-force attacks
pitfalls: Treating authentication as authorization: a logged-in user can still load other users' records unless you scope queries.

quiz.q: Why does the generator use User.authenticate_by instead of find_by(...)&.authenticate(...)?
options: It takes the same time whether or not the email exists, preventing user enumeration by timing
quiz.explain: authenticate_by always performs a password hash comparison so response time doesn't reveal valid emails.

concepts.name: Testing Rails apps
concepts.summary: Test models, controllers and full user flows with Minitest, fixtures, integration tests and system tests.
concepts.why: Rails' built-in testing stack lets you change code confidently, and every generator creates test stubs for you.
concepts.body:
Rails uses **Minitest** with Rails-specific helpers. Run everything with `bin/rails test`, a file with `bin/rails test test/models/article_test.rb`, or one test by line: `...article_test.rb:12`. Tests run in parallel and in random order, each inside a transaction that's rolled back.

Kinds of tests:

- **Model tests** (`ActiveSupport::TestCase`): validations, scopes and business methods.
- **Integration tests** (`ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest`): real HTTP requests through routes, middleware and controllers: `get articles_url`, `post articles_url, params: {...}`, then `assert_response :success`, `assert_redirected_to`, `assert_select "h1", "Articles"`.
- **System tests** (`ApplicationSystemTestCase`): drive a real browser through Capybara (`visit`, `fill_in`, `click_on`, `assert_text`). Slowest, so keep them for critical journeys.
- Job and mailer tests: `assert_enqueued_with(job: ...)`, `perform_enqueued_jobs`, `assert_emails 1`.

**Fixtures** in `test/fixtures/*.yml` load named sample records before the suite: `articles(:published)` returns one. They are fast and referenced by name, and associations can point to other fixtures by label. Many teams use factory_bot instead.

Useful helpers: `assert_difference("Article.count", 1) { ... }`, `assert_changes`, `travel_to(Time.zone.local(2025, 1, 1))`, and `sign_in_as(user)` helpers for authenticated tests.

RSpec (rspec-rails) is a popular alternative with the same concepts and a different syntax.
concepts.code:
# test/fixtures/articles.yml
# published:
#   title: Hello
#   slug: hello
#   published: true
#   author: ada          # references users(:ada)

# test/integration/articles_flow_test.rb
require "test_helper"

class ArticlesFlowTest < ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest
  setup { sign_in_as users(:ada) }     # your test helper that signs in
  test "creates an article" do
    assert_difference("Article.count", 1) do
      post articles_url, params: { article: { title: "New", body: "Text" } }
    end
    assert_redirected_to article_url(Article.last)
    follow_redirect!
    assert_select "h1", "New"
  end
  test "rejects a blank title" do
    post articles_url, params: { article: { title: "" } }
    assert_response :unprocessable_entity
  end
end
takeaways: bin/rails test runs Minitest in parallel with transactional isolation
Integration tests cover routes to views; system tests drive a real browser
Fixtures provide named sample records; assert_difference checks side effects
pitfalls: Writing mostly slow system tests for logic that model or integration tests could cover faster.

quiz.q: Which test type exercises routing, controllers and views through HTTP without a browser?
options: Unit test of the controller class
quiz.explain: ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest sends real requests through the full stack, minus JavaScript and a browser.

concepts.name: Background jobs with Active Job
concepts.summary: Run slow work in the background with Active Job and Solid Queue, with retries, scheduling and recurring tasks.
concepts.why: Emails, exports, webhooks and API calls belong in jobs so requests stay fast and failures can be retried.
concepts.body:
**Active Job** is Rails' common interface for background jobs, and **Solid Queue**, the Rails 8 default, stores jobs in the database, so no Redis is required. Sidekiq and GoodJob are popular alternative backends.

Generate a job with `bin/rails generate job ExportReport`:

```ruby
class ExportReportJob < ApplicationJob
  queue_as :default
  def perform(user, month) ... end
end
```

Enqueue with `ExportReportJob.perform_later(user, "2025-06")`. Arguments are serialised; Active Record objects are passed as **GlobalID** references and re-fetched when the job runs, so pass records rather than huge hashes. Schedule with `set(wait: 10.minutes)` or `set(wait_until: ...)`. Mailers have `deliver_later`, which uses Active Job.

Handling failure:

- `retry_on Net::OpenTimeout, wait: :polynomially_longer, attempts: 5` retries transient errors with backoff.
- `discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError` drops jobs whose records were deleted.
- Make jobs **idempotent**, since a job can run more than once after a crash or retry.

Enqueue jobs after the surrounding transaction commits (use `after_commit` callbacks), or a worker may run before the data exists.

Run workers with `bin/jobs`; in production Solid Queue can run inside Puma (`SOLID_QUEUE_IN_PUMA`) or as its own process. **Recurring tasks** are declared in `config/recurring.yml`. Mission Control Jobs adds a web dashboard for inspecting and retrying jobs. In tests, `perform_enqueued_jobs` runs them inline.
concepts.code:
class SyncInvoiceJob < ApplicationJob
  queue_as :billing
  retry_on Net::OpenTimeout, Faraday::ServerError, wait: :polynomially_longer, attempts: 5
  discard_on ActiveJob::DeserializationError       # invoice was deleted

  def perform(invoice)                              # re-fetched via GlobalID
    return if invoice.synced_at.present?            # idempotent
    remote_id = BillingApi.push(invoice.as_json)
    invoice.update!(remote_id:, synced_at: Time.current)
  end
end

class Invoice < ApplicationRecord
  after_create_commit -> { SyncInvoiceJob.perform_later(self) }
end

SyncInvoiceJob.set(wait: 10.minutes).perform_later(invoice)

# config/recurring.yml (Solid Queue)
# production:
#   nightly_cleanup:
#     class: CleanupJob
#     schedule: every day at 3am

# $ bin/jobs     # start Solid Queue workers locally
takeaways: perform_later enqueues; records are passed as GlobalIDs and reloaded
retry_on and discard_on declare failure handling; keep jobs idempotent
Solid Queue (default) stores jobs in the database; recurring tasks go in recurring.yml
pitfalls: Enqueuing a job from after_save inside a transaction, so the worker can't find the uncommitted record.

quiz.q: How does Active Job pass an Active Record object argument to a job?
options: As a JSON copy of all attributes
It can't; you must pass the id
As a GlobalID reference, re-fetching the record when the job runs
quiz.explain: GlobalID serialisation stores a reference like gid://app/Invoice/42 and loads the record at execution time.

concepts.name: Caching
concepts.summary: Speed up pages with fragment and Russian-doll caching, low-level Rails.cache, and HTTP conditional GETs.
concepts.why: Caching is the cheapest way to make a slow Rails page fast, if keys and expiry are designed correctly.
concepts.body:
Rails caching relies on **key-based expiration**: cache keys include the record's id and `updated_at` version, so when a record changes its key changes and stale entries simply stop being read. You rarely delete cache entries yourself.

**Fragment caching** in views:

```erb
<% cache article do %>
  <%= render article %>
<% end %>
```

**Russian-doll caching** nests fragments: the article fragment contains cached comment fragments. When a comment changes, `belongs_to :article, touch: true` bumps the article's `updated_at`, invalidating the outer fragment while unchanged inner fragments are reused. `render partial: "comment", collection: comments, cached: true` fetches a whole collection's fragments in one read.

**Low-level caching** stores any computed value:

```ruby
Rails.cache.fetch(["stats", user], expires_in: 12.hours) { expensive_query }
```

It returns the cached value or runs the block and stores the result. Cache plain data (numbers, hashes, arrays of ids) rather than Active Record objects or relations.

**HTTP caching**: `fresh_when(@article)` or `stale?` set ETag and Last-Modified headers, and the server answers `304 Not Modified` when the client already has the current version.

The store is configured per environment. Rails 8 uses **Solid Cache** in production, a database-backed store that can hold far more than memory-based caches; Redis and Memcached are alternatives. Caching is off in development until you run `bin/rails dev:cache`.
concepts.code:
<%# app/views/articles/show.html.erb %> <% cache @article do %> <%# key: views/articles/42-20250601... %>

<%= @article.title %>

<%= render partial: "comments/comment", collection: @article.comments, cached: true %> <% end %> <%# app/models/comment.rb: belongs_to :article, touch: true # comment change -> article updated_at bumps %> <%# app/controllers/articles_controller.rb def show @article = Article.find(params[:id]) fresh_when @article # 304 if the client's ETag matches end def stats @stats = Rails.cache.fetch(["article-stats", @article], expires_in: 1.hour) do { views: @article.views.count, readers: @article.views.distinct.count(:user_id) } end end %>
takeaways: Keys include updated_at, so changed records get new keys automatically
Russian-doll caching plus touch: true reuses unchanged inner fragments
Rails.cache.fetch caches computed values; fresh_when enables 304 responses
pitfalls: Caching relations or full Active Record objects instead of plain data, wasting space and returning stale or unloadable objects.

quiz.q: A comment is edited. With touch: true on belongs_to :article, what happens to the cached article fragment?
options: The article's updated_at changes, so its cache key changes and a new fragment is rendered
Nothing; it stays stale until it expires
quiz.explain: touch bumps the parent's timestamp, which is part of the fragment key, so the old entry is no longer used.

concepts.name: Building JSON APIs
concepts.summary: Build JSON APIs with Rails: API-only apps, rendering JSON, error handling, versioning and token authentication.
concepts.why: Rails is a productive back end for mobile apps and SPAs, and APIs need consistent responses and errors.
concepts.body:
`rails new myapi --api` creates an **API-only** app: controllers inherit from `ActionController::API`, and middleware for cookies, sessions, flash and views is left out. A regular app can serve JSON too, from the same models.

Render JSON with `render json: @article, status: :created`. By default this calls `as_json` on the object. Control the output with:

- `as_json(only: [...], include: { author: { only: :name } })` for simple cases.
- **Jbuilder** templates (`show.json.jbuilder`), which ship with Rails.
- Serializer libraries such as Alba or Blueprinter, or plain Ruby objects with a `to_h`, for larger APIs.

Never expose models wholesale, or new columns (and secrets like password digests) leak automatically.

Consistent errors: use `rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` to render a JSON 404, and return `422` with `{ errors: record.errors }` for validation failures. Use the right status codes: 201 on create, 204 with `head :no_content` on delete.

Versioning: `namespace :api do namespace :v1 do resources :articles end end` puts controllers in `Api::V1::`.

Authentication: API clients send a bearer token. `authenticate_or_request_with_http_token` reads the `Authorization: Bearer ...` header. `generates_token_for :api, expires_in: 30.days` on the model creates signed, expiring tokens that `find_by_token_for(:api, token)` verifies; for long-lived random tokens, store only a digest. Rate-limit with `rate_limit` (Rails 7.2+) and paginate collections with a gem such as Pagy or with `limit` and `offset`.
concepts.code:
# app/controllers/api/v1/articles_controller.rb
module Api::V1
  class ArticlesController < ActionController::API
    include ActionController::HttpAuthentication::Token::ControllerMethods
    before_action :authenticate!
    rescue_from ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound, with: -> { render json: { error: "not found" }, status: :not_found }

    def index
      render json: Article.published.includes(:author).limit(50)
                          .as_json(only: %i[id title], include: { author: { only: :name } })
    end

    def create
      article = @user.articles.new(params.expect(article: %i[title body]))
      if article.save then render json: article, status: :created
      else render json: { errors: article.errors }, status: :unprocessable_entity
      end
    end
    private
    def authenticate!
      @user = authenticate_with_http_token { |token, _| User.find_by_token_for(:api, token) }
      head :unauthorized unless @user
    end
  end
end
takeaways: --api apps use ActionController::API with a slimmer middleware stack
Shape JSON explicitly (as_json options, Jbuilder or serializers); don't dump models
Return proper status codes and JSON errors via rescue_from
pitfalls: Rendering models straight to JSON and leaking columns such as password_digest or internal flags.

quiz.q: What does ActionController::API leave out compared to ActionController::Base?
options: View rendering, cookies, sessions and flash support by default
quiz.explain: API controllers drop browser-oriented modules and middleware but keep params, rendering JSON and callbacks.

concepts.name: Concerns and app architecture
concepts.summary: Share behaviour with ActiveSupport::Concern, and decide when to reach for POROs, service objects and form objects.
concepts.why: As apps grow, where to put logic determines whether the codebase stays pleasant or turns into fat models and controllers.
concepts.body:
A **concern** is a module using `ActiveSupport::Concern`, kept in `app/models/concerns` or `app/controllers/concerns`. It packages a trait that several classes share, such as `Taggable`, `Searchable` or `Archivable`:

```ruby
module Archivable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  included do
    scope :archived, -> { where.not(archived_at: nil) }
  end
  class_methods do
    def archive_all = update_all(archived_at: Time.current)
  end
  def archive! = update!(archived_at: Time.current)
end
```

`included do` runs in the including class (for scopes, associations, validations and callbacks), `class_methods` adds class methods, and plain methods become instance methods. Concerns can depend on other concerns, and Concern resolves the include order for you.

Concerns are good for genuine, cohesive roles. They are bad as a way to hide a 2,000-line model in five files.

Beyond models and controllers, Rails is happy with plain Ruby objects in `app/models` or new directories under `app/` (all autoloaded):

- **Domain objects (POROs)** for concepts without a table, e.g. `Invoice::Calculator`.
- **Form objects** with `ActiveModel::Model` and `ActiveModel::Attributes` for forms that span several models or have no table, getting validations and `form_with` support.
- **Service or command objects** for multi-step workflows (`Checkout.new(cart, user).call`), when the work doesn't clearly belong to one model.
- **Query objects** for complex reporting queries.

Prefer rich models first; extract only when a class has several unrelated responsibilities.
concepts.code:
module Archivable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  included do
    scope :archived, -> { where.not(archived_at: nil) }
  end
  class_methods do
    def archive_older_than(age) = where(created_at: ...age.ago).update_all(archived_at: Time.current)
  end
  def archive! = update!(archived_at: Time.current)
end

class Article < ApplicationRecord; include Archivable; end

class Signup                      # form object spanning User + Account
  include ActiveModel::Model
  attr_accessor :email_address, :company
  validates :email_address, :company, presence: true
  def save
    return false unless valid?
    ActiveRecord::Base.transaction do
      account = Account.create!(name: company)
      account.users.create!(email_address:, password: SecureRandom.base58(24))
    end
  end
end
takeaways: ActiveSupport::Concern: included do for class-level macros, class_methods for class methods
Use concerns for cohesive shared roles, not to hide oversized classes
POROs, form objects and service objects live happily in app/ and are autoloaded
pitfalls: Splitting one bloated model into many single-use concerns, which spreads complexity instead of reducing it.

quiz.q: Inside an ActiveSupport::Concern, where should scope :archived go?
quiz.explain: included do runs in the context of the including class, where scope and other macros are available.

concepts.name: Autoloading, Zeitwerk and boot
concepts.summary: Understand how Zeitwerk maps files to constants, how reloading and eager loading work, and the Rails boot process.
concepts.why: Autoloading errors and boot-time mistakes are confusing until you know the rules Zeitwerk follows.
concepts.body:
Rails apps never `require` their own files. **Zeitwerk** maps file paths under autoload directories (`app/*` subdirectories, `lib` via `config.autoload_lib`) to constants by convention: `app/models/user_profile.rb` must define `UserProfile`, and `app/services/billing/invoice_sync.rb` must define `Billing::InvoiceSync`. Directories become namespaces. Acronyms need an inflection rule (`inflect.acronym "API"`) if you want `API` rather than `Api`.

Modes:

- **Development**: constants load lazily on first reference, and when files change Rails **reloads** them by removing the autoloaded constants and starting fresh on the next request. Never keep references to reloadable classes in places that survive reloads, such as initializers or class-level caches; use `Rails.application.config.to_prepare` for setup that must run after each reload.
- **Production and tests in CI**: everything is **eager loaded** at boot, which is thread-safe, catches naming errors early and plays well with copy-on-write forking.

Run `bin/rails zeitwerk:check` to verify every file defines the expected constant.

**Boot sequence**: `config/boot.rb` sets up Bundler (and Bootsnap's load-path cache), `config/application.rb` requires the frameworks and defines your `Application` class, `config/environments/*.rb` applies per-environment settings, then **initializers** in `config/initializers` run in alphabetical order, and **Railties** (engines and gems) hook in with their own initializers. Finally, eager loading happens if enabled and the app is ready to serve.

Keep initializers small and side-effect free; heavy work there slows every boot, test run and deploy.
concepts.code:
# File -> constant mapping that Zeitwerk expects
# app/models/user_profile.rb             -> UserProfile
# app/models/billing/invoice.rb          -> Billing::Invoice
# app/services/payments/stripe_client.rb -> Payments::StripeClient
# lib/pdf_renderer.rb (autoload_lib)     -> PdfRenderer

# config/application.rb
module Blog
  class Application < Rails::Application
    config.load_defaults 8.0
    config.autoload_lib(ignore: %w[assets tasks])
  end
end

# config/initializers/inflections.rb
ActiveSupport::Inflector.inflections(:en) { |i| i.acronym "API" }
# now app/controllers/api/users_controller.rb -> API::UsersController

# config/initializers/payments.rb
Rails.application.config.to_prepare do
  Payments.gateway = Payments::StripeClient.new   # re-run after each code reload
end
# $ bin/rails zeitwerk:check
# Hold on, I am eager loading the application.
# All is good!
takeaways: Zeitwerk maps file paths to constant names; directories are namespaces
Development autoloads and reloads; production eager loads at boot
Use to_prepare for setup that references reloadable classes; check with zeitwerk:check
pitfalls: Storing a reference to an app class in an initializer, which becomes stale after a reload in development.

quiz.q: app/services/pdf/export.rb defines class PdfExport. What happens?
options: Zeitwerk expects Pdf::Export there and raises a naming error when loading
quiz.explain: Zeitwerk derives the expected constant from the path; a mismatch fails, and zeitwerk:check reports it.

concepts.name: Rack and the middleware stack
concepts.summary: See how a request travels from Puma through Rack middleware and the router to a controller, and write your own middleware.
concepts.why: Understanding Rack explains cookies, sessions, CSRF and logging, and lets you add cross-cutting behaviour cleanly.
concepts.body:
**Rack** is the interface between Ruby web servers and frameworks. A Rack app is any object with `call(env)` that returns `[status, headers, body]`, where `env` is a hash describing the request. Rails itself is a Rack app, started from `config.ru`.

A request's journey:

- **Puma** accepts the connection and builds the `env`. In production Rails 8 apps, **Thruster** sits in front of Puma, adding HTTP/2, compression, asset caching and X-Sendfile.
- The **middleware stack**: each middleware wraps the next, can modify the `env`, short-circuit with its own response, or modify the response on the way back. `bin/rails middleware` lists them: `ActionDispatch::HostAuthorization`, `Rack::Sendfile`, `ActionDispatch::Static`, `ActionDispatch::Executor`, `Rack::Runtime`, `ActionDispatch::RequestId`, `Rails::Rack::Logger`, `ActionDispatch::ShowExceptions`, `ActionDispatch::Cookies`, `ActionDispatch::Session::CookieStore`, `ActionDispatch::Flash`, `Rack::MethodOverride`, `Rack::ETag` and more.
- The **router** (`ActionDispatch::Routing::RouteSet`, also a Rack app) matches the path and calls the controller action, itself a Rack endpoint.

Add your own middleware with `config.middleware.use MyMiddleware`, or position it with `insert_before`/`insert_after`, and remove one with `config.middleware.delete`. Middleware fits concerns that apply to every request regardless of controller: request timing, tenant detection from the host, blocking abusive IPs (often via `rack-attack`), or adding headers.

Routes can also mount any Rack app directly: `mount Sidekiq::Web => "/sidekiq"` or `mount ->(env) { [200, {}, ["ok"]] } => "/ping"`.
concepts.code:
# app/middleware/request_timer.rb
class RequestTimer
  def initialize(app) = @app = app
  def call(env)
    started = Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
    status, headers, body = @app.call(env)              # inner layers + Rails
    ms = ((Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC) - started) * 1000).round(1)
    headers["server-timing"] = "app;dur=#{ms}"
    [status, headers, body]
  end
end
# config/application.rb
#   config.middleware.insert_before Rack::Runtime, RequestTimer
# config/routes.rb: any Rack app can be mounted
#   mount ->(env) { [200, { "content-type" => "text/plain" }, ["pong"]] }, at: "/ping"
# $ bin/rails middleware
# use ActionDispatch::HostAuthorization
# use Rack::Sendfile
# use ActionDispatch::Static
# use ActionDispatch::Executor
# ...
# use RequestTimer
# use Rack::Runtime
# ...
# run Blog::Application.routes
takeaways: A Rack app is call(env) returning [status, headers, body]
Rails is a middleware stack wrapped around the router; bin/rails middleware lists it
Use middleware for cross-cutting, controller-independent behaviour
pitfalls: Putting per-request logic that needs current_user or params into middleware; it runs before routing and controllers.

quiz.q: What must a Rack middleware's call(env) return?
quiz.explain: The Rack spec requires a status, a headers hash and an enumerable body.

concepts.name: Deployment, Puma and performance
concepts.summary: Deploy with Kamal 2, tune Puma workers and threads, size connection pools, and find production bottlenecks.
concepts.why: Production capacity, latency and reliability depend on process and thread settings as much as on code.
concepts.body:
Rails 8 apps are deployed as Docker containers with **Kamal 2**. `config/deploy.yml` lists servers, the image registry and environment secrets (`.kamal/secrets`). `kamal setup` prepares fresh servers, and `kamal deploy` builds the image, pushes it, boots new containers and switches traffic through **kamal-proxy** with zero downtime and automatic Let's Encrypt TLS. Accessories run databases or Redis next to the app. Heroku, Render and Fly.io remain alternatives.

**Puma** serves requests with processes and threads:

- `WEB_CONCURRENCY` sets **workers** (forked processes). Use roughly one per CPU core for real parallelism, since the GVL lets only one thread run Ruby at a time per process.
- `RAILS_MAX_THREADS` sets **threads** per worker (default 3 since Rails 7.2). Threads overlap I/O waits (database, HTTP) but compete for the GVL, so more threads raises throughput and also latency.
- `preload_app!` loads the app before forking so workers share memory via copy-on-write.

The database **connection pool** (`pool:` in `database.yml`) must be at least the number of threads that use the database in each process, including Solid Queue threads if they run inside Puma; otherwise threads wait for connections and time out.

Production checklist: enable YJIT (on by default when available), serve assets with long cache headers via Thruster or a CDN, keep jobs off the web process for heavy loads, and watch p95 and p99 latency, not averages. Find bottlenecks with an APM or open-source tools: `rack-mini-profiler`, query logs with `config.active_record.query_log_tags_enabled`, and `bin/rails` logs showing time spent in views versus Active Record.
concepts.code:
# config/deploy.yml (Kamal 2, abridged)
service: blog
image: acme/blog
servers:
  web: [203.0.113.10, 203.0.113.11]
  job:
    hosts: [203.0.113.12]
    cmd: bin/jobs
proxy:
  ssl: true
  host: blog.example.com
env:
  clear:
    WEB_CONCURRENCY: 4      # ~1 Puma worker per core
    RAILS_MAX_THREADS: 3    # threads per worker
  secret: [RAILS_MASTER_KEY]

# config/database.yml (production excerpt)
#   pool: <%= ENV.fetch("RAILS_MAX_THREADS") { 3 } %>

# $ kamal setup     # first time: install Docker, boot kamal-proxy, deploy
# $ kamal deploy    # zero-downtime rollout
# $ kamal app logs -f
takeaways: Kamal 2 deploys Docker images with zero downtime through kamal-proxy
Puma workers give parallelism; threads overlap I/O within the GVL
Size the DB pool to at least the threads per process that use the database
pitfalls: Raising RAILS_MAX_THREADS without raising the database pool, causing connection timeouts under load.

quiz.q: A server has 4 cores and CPU-heavy requests. What most increases parallel throughput?
options: More Puma workers (about one per core)
quiz.explain: The GVL limits each process to one running Ruby thread, so parallel CPU work needs more processes.

quiz.q: Puma runs 5 threads per worker and Solid Queue runs 3 threads in the same process. What's the minimum sensible pool size?
quiz.explain: Every thread that may query the database at once needs its own connection: 5 + 3 = 8.
